'''Carol Ruckdeschel''' is a [[biologist]], [[naturalist]], [[environmental activist]]<ref>{{cite news|authorlink=John McPhee|url=http://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1973/04/28/travels-in-georgia|title=Travels in Georgia|last=McPhee|first=John|date=April 28, 1973|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|accessdate=September 23, 2014}}</ref> and author. As a [[Cumberland Island]] resident, she was involved in the creation and preservation of [[Cumberland Island National Seashore]].<ref name="Dilsaver2004">{{cite book|last=Dilsaver|first=Lary M.|title=Cumberland Island National Seashore: A History of Conservation Conflict|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wfjrDw09GaEC&pg=PA128|accessdate=September 23, 2014|year=2004|publisher=University of Virginia Press|isbn=9780813922683|pages=128–}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book| edition = First | publisher = Grove Press| isbn = 9780802122582| last = Harlan| first = Will| title = Untamed: the wildest woman in America and the fight for Cumberland Island| location = New York| date = 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news| last = Blqackmun| first = Susie| title = The Naturalist For 16 Hours A Day, Seven Days A Week, Biologist Carol Ruckdeschel Lives Breathes, Studies And Defends A Tiny Barrier Island Just Over The Florida Border. It's Not Just A Job, It's A Way Of Life That She Has Followed For Nearly 20 Years| access-date = April 19, 2015| date = June 9, 1991| url = https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1991/06/09/the-naturalist-for-16-hours-a-day-seven-days-a-week-biologist-carol-ruckdeschel-lives-breathes-studies-and-defends-a-tiny-barrier-island-just-over-the-florida-border-its-not-just-a-job-its-a-way-of-life-that-she-has-followed-for-nearly-20-years/}}</ref> She is the subject of the book ''[[Untamed: The Wildest Woman in America and the Fight for Cumberland Island]]'' by Will Harlan.

She has researched [[sea turtles]]<ref>Sea Turtles of the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of the United States. Carol Ruckdeschel. 2006</ref> and endangered and extinct species around the Georgia coast.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/the-bone-collectors-37287990/|title=History, Travel, Arts, Science, People, Places – Smithsonian|publisher=Smithsonianmag.com|accessdate=November 26, 2014}}</ref>

Her residence on the north part of [[Cumberland Island]] is currently owned by The [[National Park Service]], on the condition of her remaining there until her death.<ref name=":0" />

* Robert Shoop, C., and Carol Ruckdeschel. "Increasing turtle strandings in the southeast United States: a complicating factor." ''Biological Conservation'' 23.3 (1982): 213–215.
* Frazier, J. G., Judith E. Winston, and Carol A. Ruckdeschel. "Epizoan communities on marine turtles. III. Bryozoa." ''Bulletin of marine science'' 51.1 (1992): 1–8.
